extra.message: User-controlled 'username' path parameter (from api_views/users.py get_by_username) is interpolated directly into a raw SQL string via f-string and executed with db.session.execute(text(user_query)). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, e.g. ' OR '1'='1, to bypass queries and dump the users table.

The Flask SECRET_KEY used to sign JWT auth tokens (models/user_model.py encode_auth_token/decode_auth_token) is hardcoded to the trivial value 'random'. Anyone who reads the source can forge valid HS256 JWTs for any user, including admins, completely bypassing authentication.

register_user trusts the client-supplied 'admin' field from the JSON body (request_data['admin']) and passes it to the User constructor, allowing any unauthenticated registrant to create an admin account and escalate privileges (admins can delete arbitrary users via delete_user).

The GET /users/v1/_debug endpoint (api_views.users.debug) has no authentication (no bearerAuth in openapi3.yml and no token_validator call) and returns User.get_all_users_debug(), which via User.json_debug (models/user_model.py:58-59) discloses every user's username, plaintext password, email and admin flag.

extra.message: get_by_title fetches a book solely by book_title without verifying that the book belongs to the authenticated user (Book.query.filter_by(book_title=...) with no user filter), and returns its secret_content. Any authenticated user can read the secret of any other user's book (broken object level authorization / IDOR).

extra.message: update_password looks up the user by the 'username' URL path parameter (attacker-controlled) instead of the authenticated identity from the JWT (resp['sub']), then sets that user's password (line 189). Any authenticated user can change the password of any other account, including the admin, achieving full account takeover.

Any unauthenticated remote attacker can wipe all users/books at will (destructive action / denial of service).

extra.message: get_by_username (GET /users/v1/{username}) performs no token validation and the OpenAPI spec assigns it no bearerAuth security, so any unauthenticated attacker can query arbitrary usernames and learn whether accounts exist (and retrieve their email addresses), enabling user enumeration.

extra.message: Passwords are stored in cleartext: the User model assigns self.password = password with no hashing, and login compares request_data.get('password') == user.password directly (api_views/users.py:93). A database or debug-endpoint leak immediately compromises all credentials.

cwe: CWE-256: Plaintext Storage of a Password

extra.message: login_user returns a distinct response ('Username does not exist') when the supplied username is not registered, versus a different message for a wrong password. This observable response discrepancy lets attackers enumerate valid usernames.

login_user returns 'Password is not correct for the given username.' when the username exists but the password is wrong, confirming account validity to attackers and enabling targeted credential attacks.

update_email applies the nested-quantifier regular expression ^([0-9a-zA-Z]([-.\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])*@{1}([0-9a-zA-Z][-\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z]\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,9})$ to attacker-controlled email input via re.search. Crafted input causes catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS), consuming CPU and denying service.

The application runs with debug=True on host 0.0.0.0, exposing the Werkzeug interactive debugger on all interfaces. The debugger permits arbitrary Python code execution in the context of the server, leading to remote code execution, and also leaks stack traces and configuration.

init_db_users seeds the database with a hardcoded administrator account with well-known credentials (username 'admin', password 'pass1'). Any deployment using the default seed data grants attackers immediate admin access.
